title: LoRa-MQTT Geofencing Notification System for Maritime Boundary Violations on Indonesian Fishing Vessels

authors.name: Putu Satya Wirananda
authors.affiliation: Automation Engineering Technology Study Program, Department of Industrial Technology, Vocational School, Diponegoro University

authors.name: Ahmad Ridlo Hanifudin Tahier
authors.affiliation: Automation Engineering Technology Study Program, Department of Industrial Technology, Vocational School, Diponegoro University

abstract: Maritime boundary violations by traditional fishing vessels threaten resource sustainability and diplomatic relations around Indonesian borders, especially in regions such as North Natuna and Java Sea. Prior low-cost alarm prototypes using Neo-6M and Arduino gave local alerts but could not report violations to shore or maintain multi-hop links [4]. We present a LoRa-MQTT geofencing notification system that integrates Neo-M8N GPS, SX1278 LoRa, and ESP32-based transmitters, repeaters, and a gateway to detect line-crossing events and forward them to an MQTT broker and HTML dashboard. Innovations include (1) a chained LoRa repeater topology for multi-hop reach to 3 km with gateway handoff, (2) a deterministic line-crossing algorithm (D and S) for Safe/Alert/Violation decisions, and (3) lightweight JSON payloads and MQTT publish/subscribe for real-time visualization. Field results: Neo-M8N mean position error = 1.62 m and cold start 5–7 s; Neo-6M mean error = 3.04 m and cold start up to 525 s. LoRa performance: stable up to 2 km with 0% packet loss and mean latency 1.55 s; at 3 km packet loss rose to 20.63% (north coast) and 13.2% (south coast noisy). The geofence classifier achieved 95.4% accuracy and F1 = 0.947 for the three-zone vocabulary. This low-power, low-cost prototype enables remote monitoring of traditional vessels and provides an actionable tool for maritime authorities to detect and record boundary transgressions in remote Indonesian waters.

content.text: Indonesia's coastline and archipelagic configuration make maritime monitoring a persistent operational challenge for the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries and local coast guards in regions such as North Natuna and the Java Sea, where traditional fishing vessels operate close to international borders. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing and accidental boundary crossings have produced diplomatic incidents and local safety risks (2015–2023 statistics show dozens to hundreds of annual incidents) [1], [2]. Local skippers often lack modern navigation aids and formal instruction about UNCLOS 1982 limits (12 nautical miles), so transgressions can be unintentional and unnoticed. The consequence is not only lost stock but potential detention of boats and uneasy bilateral negotiations.

Several prior works tackled low-cost boundary alarms and vessel tracking. Rahmad et al. [1] provided a geographic analysis of Indonesia–Malaysia sea borders using GIS; they mapped zones but did not implement on-vessel alarms. Hadi and Arsana [4] built a Neo-6M/Arduino alarm that sounded locally and achieved in-lab detection but lacked remote reporting and recorded logs; their device's accuracy was not quantified beyond observational remarks. Apriani et al. [5] demonstrated LoRa SX1278 based vessel tracking with 89.2% message delivery at 1 km on calm coasts but reported significant packet loss at 3 km. National reports and briefings [2], [3] document seizure counts (e.g., 212 vessels in 2022) but do not propose an embedded system for small-scale vessels. These gaps point toward the need for an integrated, field-tested hardware/software prototype that both alerts crews and transmits validated events to shore.

The specific unsolved problem here is measurable: earlier low-cost alarms either fail to report events off-boat or show position errors exceeding 3 m and acquisition delays exceeding 300 s (Neo-6M cold start), which makes near-boundary classification unreliable. In practice, a device that yields positional error above 3 m can misclassify a vessel as 'Violation' when it is inside the safe band (the design target is classification accuracy > 90% and response latency under 2 s for reporting). Also, LoRa single-hop tests earlier reported near 100% success only on calm coasts up to 1 km, while repeaters and MQTT integration were not evaluated in mixed coastal noise.

We therefore propose a complete system and field validation. The contributions are: 
• A prototype three-node LoRa chain (Transmitter, Repeater, Receiver/Gateway) with ESP32 and SX1278 that preserves data integrity up to multi-hop 3 km, and measured latency and packet-loss statistics (target: latency \leq 2 s, success \geq 90% at 2 km). 
• A geofencing classifier based on Cartesian line-crossing (D) and perpendicular distance (S) with an operational decision logic that yields 95.4% geofence classification accuracy in field trials. 
• A practical hardware selection and enclosure design for small fishing boats (Neo-M8N for position, 18650 battery pack, compact PCB) with power budgets and battery life measurements: transmitter endurance 6.3 h, repeater 17.1 h, receiver 16 h. 
• End-to-end software integration: lightweight JSON payloads, MQTT broker, Python subscriber storing to MySQL, and an HTML/PHP dashboard with real-time map, RSSI/SNR plots, and alarm logic.

Section II reviews related work in three threads: boundary studies and GIS [1], on-vessel alarm prototypes and GPS modules [4], and LoRa/MQTT ship telemetry [5], [6]. Section III details the system design: hardware, messages, geofence math, and software. Section IV presents field experiments on two coasts (north and south), accuracy and communication measurements, and comparison to prior methods. Section V concludes with limitations and specific next steps for deployment and research.

This section examines three literature threads that connect to our system: (A) maritime boundary analyses and GIS approaches that define the problem space, (B) low-cost on-vessel alarm and GPS sensor research that motivates hardware selection, and (C) long-range low-power communication and IoT integration (LoRa and MQTT) for remote monitoring. Each thread highlights concrete findings and limits that our work addresses.

section2a.title: Topic Thread A — Maritime Boundary Analysis and GIS

content.text: Rahmad et al. [1] performed a GIS-based geographic study of the Indonesia–Malaysia sea border using nautical charts and produced a spatial baseline and buffer maps; their result quantified ambiguous baselines in several straits but did not instrument vessels for live alerts (their system is desktop GIS only). The key metric was a mapped baseline accuracy to chart datum ±10 m in survey regions, and the limitation is an absence of embedded on-vessel enforcement or alerting. This means offline maps alone can't prevent accidental crossings. Hadi and Arsana [4] prototyped an Arduino + Neo-6M alarm; they reported local audible warnings but no logged event, and their cold-start times exceeded 300 s in obstructed locations (their note: cold-start up to 525 s), which reduces practical usefulness near busy shorelines. Our work builds on these by moving from offline maps and local-only alarms to an integrated alert-and-report chain that records events and forwards them to shore.

Mo et al. [6] examined digital twins and HMI for coastal surveillance using OPC-UA and SCADA, reporting telemetry fidelity at 250 ms update intervals in controlled networks but noting that field-wide deployments require edge aggregation and lower-bandwidth links to scale. This limitation motivates our choice of MQTT for brokered, low-bandwidth reporting. Apriani et al. [5] showed LoRa-based vessel tracking and reported 89.2% packet delivery at 1 km with an SX1278 on shore, but at 3 km their delivery fell below 80% depending on antenna choice; they concluded single-hop LoRa requires either stronger antennas or repeaters. Our repeater topology directly responds to that gap by preserving payloads over two hops in noisy coastal conditions.

section2b.title: Topic Thread B — On-Vessel GPS and Alarm Prototypes

content.text: This subsection reviews design- and sensor-level studies that informed component choices. Hadi and Arsana [4] tested Neo-6M modules on small craft and reported in-situ observable cold-start delays of several minutes under tree canopy and dock-side obstructions (their cold-start metric: up to 525 s under heavy obstruction). They documented average position deviations in the 2.8–4.0 m range but did not publish a statistical RMSE. Chen et al. [7] compared u-blox M8-series (Neo-M8N) against low-cost modules in trials and reported mean error 1.5–2.0 m and TTFF (time to first fix) 5–7 s in open-sky conditions; the limitation they noted was higher current draw during continuous fix acquisition (impacts battery life). This finding directly motivated our battery and power-measurement plans.

Sen and colleagues [8] evaluated smartphone GNSS augmentation and showed sub-meter relative accuracy in urban conditions using combined GNSS+SBAS corrections but noted that phones need cellular or internet to fetch corrections; their mean accuracy advantage was 0.7 m over standalone modules. For low-cost boat installations, however, relying on cellular coverage is not reliable. Kim et al. [9] surveyed GPS modules in marine environments and concluded that M8-family receivers consistently outperformed Neo-6M in multipath scenarios but demanded an external patch antenna and improved filtering to achieve the quoted accuracy. These precise hardware trade-offs led us to compare Neo-6M and Neo-M8N under identical enclosure and antenna conditions and to choose Neo-M8N as primary despite slightly higher cost (roughly 2–3x), because field accuracy and TTFF were decisive.

Finally, Prado et al. [10] implemented a buzzer-based local alarm and recorded false-alert rates near 7% when GPS jitter exceeded 4 m. They recommended fusing a short-term filter and a hysteresis band around the geofence line. Our contribution addresses this by using both determinant sign (D) and minimum distance (S) together with short temporal hysteresis to reduce false alarms.

section2c.title: Topic Thread C — LoRa, MQTT and Edge Reporting

content.text: The third thread reviews low-power wide-area networks and brokered telemetry systems for maritime contexts. Apriani et al. [5] implemented LoRa SX1278 onboard and reported 89.2% delivery at 1 km and significant drops past 2 km without external antennas. They used single-hop topologies; their limitation motivates multi-hop repeaters. Yashika et al. [11] demonstrated MediaPipe gesture recognition and offload to PLCs using MQTT and noted message latencies under 300 ms on local networks but did not measure over LoRa. For maritime monitoring, MQTT provides a simple topic structure and QoS settings that fit our JSON-payload needs, but again it relies on the radio link to the broker.

Bosch Rexroth documentation and Bosch field notes on EtherCAT and industrial I/O [12] point out that wired systems can reach deterministic cycles; but coastal and shipboard contexts require wireless hop aggregation and graceful degradation. Recent field studies [13], [14] evaluated LoRa performance across water paths and found that coastal contour and sea state (wave height, spray) degrade RSSI and SNR by several dB relative to calm inland fields, with packet loss rising above 10% past 2 km under high-wave conditions. Those studies measured RSSI deltas of 4–6 dB and recommended repeater placement and antenna tuning for resilience. Our experiments mirror these findings and quantify them for Indonesian north and south coasts.

Synthesis: across all threads the collective gap remains the absence of a field-proven, low-cost, on-vessel device that both warns the crew locally and reliably forwards signed geofence events to a central broker over noisy coastal channels. We address this by combining Neo-M8N accuracy, a two-hop SX1278 repeater chain, and MQTT-based event logging and visualization.

This section describes the end-to-end prototype: hardware, physical packaging for fishing vessels, the geofencing math used to classify crossings, message formats and MQTT flows, and the experimental constraints that shaped the design. The system was required to run on 18650 battery packs, operate for multiple hours unattended, and report events to a coastal MQTT broker via WiFi at the gateway. Power, range, and classification latency were the key design constraints that determined module choices and software architecture.

The architecture is a three-tiered chain: a Transmitter node mounted on the fishing vessel, an optional on-route Repeater node for range extension, and a Receiver/Gateway on an onshore mast or monitoring boat that bridges to an MQTT broker via ESP32 WiFi. The Transmitter collects GNSS position (Neo-M8N or Neo-6M), computes the D and S geofence metrics locally, and emits a compact JSON payload via SX1278 at 433 MHz. The Repeater listens, forwards the packet unchanged, and preserves header addressing. The Gateway receives the forwarded packet, publishes to an MQTT broker at QoS 1, and a Python subscriber writes messages to a MySQL table. The dashboard (HTML/PHP) queries the database and renders maps and signal plots. This structure was chosen because it minimises packet processing on repeater nodes, reduces end-to-end latency by avoiding store-and-forward processing, and keeps the transmitter power budget low by using short transmit bursts.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the transmitter performs sensing, geofence decision, and short-burst radio transmission, while the repeater does a transparent forward operation to conserve energy and timing. The novel decision here is the minimal processing performed by the repeater; this reduces its average on-air time and simplifies recovery after interference. The gateway's WiFi link to the broker was chosen because coastal monitoring stations typically have intermittent wired infrastructure but can host a WiFi-enabled mast (ESP32) close to the shore.

In (1), D is the 2D point-line determinant that indicates which side of the boundary line the vessel point P lies on. Variables: x_A, y_A and x_B, y_B are the geofence boundary endpoints (degrees of latitude and longitude, deg), x_P, y_P are the vessel coordinates (deg). D is unitless but its sign indicates side; typical D magnitude ranges from 10^{-8} to 10^{-4} in our sample because lat/lon are small decimals. We chose this planar determinant formulation because it is computationally cheap and stable for short coastal segments where spherical curvature can be neglected (distances < 10 km).

Hardware choices balanced cost, energy, and real-world accuracy. The Transmitter uses an ESP32-WROOM for MCU and WiFi provisioning, a u-blox Neo-M8N GNSS module for primary position, an SX1278 Ra-02 LoRa module for radio, a small active patch antenna (2.4 dBi) tuned for 433 MHz, and a 2×18650 battery pack with a 5 V step-up converter. Repeaters and the receiver use the same radio with higher-gain antennas for the hop toward shore. All electronics are mounted on a custom two-layer PCB inside an IP65-rated box with cable glands for the antenna and power. The hardware selection was driven by three requirements: low power (multiple-hour runtime on 18650 cells), compact form factor for small boats, and the ability to field-upgrade firmware via the gateway.

content.text: As shown in Table I, we selected the Neo-M8N over Neo-6M for its TTFF and accuracy despite higher cost (Neo-M8N module unit price roughly IDR 150–200k versus Neo-6M IDR 40–80k at the time of procurement). The ESP32 was chosen instead of an Arduino Uno because it provides native WiFi for the gateway and a higher processing budget for JSON formatting, plus lower power modes and hardware timers. The SX1278 Ra-02 was chosen because 433 MHz propagation over water is favorable and off-the-shelf Ra-02 modules are widely available and cheap.

content.text: The geofencing algorithm runs on the Transmitter and on the Gateway for redundancy. It implements line-crossing detection: compute determinant D (sign indicates side), compute perpendicular distance S to the line, apply hysteresis over a 3-s sliding window to suppress transient jitter, and output one of three states: Safe, Alert, Violation. Messages are sent as compact JSON with eight fields: id, lat, lon, status, tstamp, RSSI, SNR, and seq. The Transmitter sends at a configurable interval (default 5 s) or immediately if status transitions to Violation. Acknowledgement is not required from the gateway, but repeaters forward packets with header preservation. This approach balances energy with timeliness.

As given by (2), S is the perpendicular distance from point P to the line AB. Variables: D is from (1) (unitless), x_A,y_A and x_B,y_B are line endpoints in degrees, and R_{\mathrm{deg2m}} is the conversion factor from degree differences to meters along the local latitude (approx. 111,320 m per degree latitude; for longitude use 111,320\cos(\phi) m per degree). We include R_{\mathrm{deg2m}} to convert the planar determinant into meters for operational thresholds. Typical S values used in classification were: S > 1000 m -> Safe, 20 m < S \leq 1000 m -> Alert, S \leq 20 m and D < 0 -> Violation.

Equation (3) defines battery endurance estimate t_{\mathrm{bat}} in hours. Here C is battery capacity in mAh (2,400 mAh), and I_{\mathrm{avg}} is average current in mA for the device role. For the transmitter we measured I_{\mathrm{avg}} \approx 380 mA, giving t_{\mathrm{bat}} \approx 6.3 h; for the repeater I_{\mathrm{avg}} \approx 140 mA giving \approx17.1 h. This simple linear model omits Peukert effects and step-up converter losses, but it matched measured endurance within 5% in our trials.

content.text: Communication uses SX1278 at 433 MHz for the air link and MQTT over TCP/IP for shore-side storage. The transmitter sends JSON payloads over LoRa with SF10 for robust links at long range; repeater forwards unchanged. The gateway ESP32 subscribes to the local serial port from SX1278, wraps payloads into MQTT messages, and publishes to broker at topic "vessel/+/telemetry". The broker runs QoS 1 to trade reliability and latency. Packet format is: {"id":"V001","lat":-6.905398,"lon":110.498553,"status":"Alert","t":"2024-10-03T17:01:24Z","rssi":-82,"snr":6,"seq":124}. Scan cycle constraints: transmitter sleep-to-send cycle is 5 s default; MQTT publish time measured under local WiFi was < 20 ms. Header addressing uses a 3-byte source/dest pair to ensure repeaters forward only intended packets.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 5, the design keeps LoRa and MQTT responsibilities separate: LoRa for last-mile maritime hops; MQTT for brokered storage and multi-client subscription. Timing constraints in (4) guided component selection: scan cycles must keep average end-to-end latency under 2 s for practical monitoring, and WiFi-to-broker latency must remain low so dashboards update near real-time.

Equation (4) breaks down round-trip or end-to-end latency. T_{\mathrm{tx}} is LoRa airtime and transmit scheduling (ms to 1 s depending on SF), T_{\mathrm{prop}} is propagation (negligible over kilometers, <1 ms), T_{\mathrm{proc}} is node processing (tens of ms), and T_{\mathrm{rx}} is gateway-to-broker and storage latency (tens to hundreds of ms). For our measurements the mean T_{\mathrm{RTT}} was about 1.55 s (1550 ms) for two-hop chains up to 2 km on the north coast.

This section reports field trials on two contrasting Indonesian coasts (a calmer north coast and a high-noise south coast). Tests measured GPS accuracy (Neo-6M vs Neo-M8N), LoRa two-hop performance (RSSI, SNR, packet loss, latency), battery endurance, and geofence classification accuracy. Trials included 50+ packets per distance point and repeated runs under both open-sky and obstacle-cluster conditions to ensure statistical reliability.

Field experiments were performed near Semarang (Central Java) and two coastal sites chosen for differing sea states: the North Coast (calm, sheltered) and the South Coast (open sea, higher waves). Equipment used: three prototype devices (Transmitter, Repeater, Receiver), a laptop with Arduino IDE and Python logger, a smartphone for GPS reference, a handheld multimeter to measure battery voltage, and a stopwatch for TTFF timing. Tests included cold-start and warm-start GNSS measurements, static and short-mobile LoRa range tests at 10 m, 250 m, 500 m, 750 m, 1 km, 2 km, and 3 km. Each distance test sent a minimum of 50 packets per run. Software versions: ESP-IDF 4.4 for ESP32 firmware, Python 3.9 for logger, Mosquitto 2.0 broker on a Raspberry Pi 4, PHP 8.0 for dashboard server. Environmental conditions (air temp, wind speed, wave height) were logged for each run to correlate with signal metrics.

As shown in Table II, the transmitter defaulted to a 5 s send interval (0.2 Hz) to balance timeliness and battery life; we ran 50-trial batches per distance to estimate packet loss probabilities with reasonable confidence. The 125 kHz bandwidth with SF10 was chosen to increase link resilience at 2+ km while keeping airtime acceptable (subsecond to few-second airtime depending on payload size). The load condition labeled 100% refers to the transmitter actively sending at the configured interval with GPS and radio modules powered.

content.text: Headline: LoRa two-hop transfer maintained an average end-to-end latency of 1.55 s and 0% packet loss up to 2 km on the North Coast; accuracy of the geofence classifier reached 95.4% over the test corpus. This performance results from the Neo-M8N position stability (mean error 1.62 m) and the repeater's transparent forwarding which preserved packet timing. We measured three factors that explain the outcomes: GNSS TTFF and accuracy (which affect classification), LoRa link budget and antenna gain (which affect packet loss), and firmware send/forward timing (which affects latency).

Table III shows that the classification accuracy exceeded the 90% target. The primary cause was the Neo-M8N's smaller mean positional error (1.62 m) compared with Neo-6M (3.04 m); smaller error reduces ambiguous samples near the boundary and thus reduces false alarms. The latency metric met the design constraint (1.55 s < 2 s), mostly because our repeater design forwarded packets immediately without buffering. An anomaly worth noting: in one south-coast run with wave heights above 1.5 m and gusting wind, SNR dropped by 6 dB and packet loss rose to 13.2% at 2 km, which means that severe sea states can impair reporting even with multi-hop. In deployment terms, the system is dependable for routine monitoring and early warning, but not a complete replacement for patrol ships in high-sea emergency conditions.

content.text: Fig. 7 illustrates that the achieved accuracy and F1 exceed the targets while latency and power remain within budgets. The most interesting observation is that classification accuracy improved more than expected after we added a 3-s hysteresis; this reduced short-lived GNSS jitter from causing false Violation triggers. What this means for deployment is that a modest temporal filter can substantially reduce false alarms, which operational teams appreciate (they don't want unnecessary vessel stops).

Equation (5) defines the F1-score used to summarise classification balance. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) and Recall = TP/(TP+FN). In our test corpus Precision = 0.951 and Recall = 0.943, giving F1 = 0.947. These values indicate the classifier is slightly more precise than recall, which operationally is acceptable since a missed violation (false negative) is rarer but carries higher consequence; in our application the observed slight imbalance was mitigated by automatic re-sampling and event escalation at the gateway.

Headline: Our prototype reached 95.4% accuracy and 1.55 s latency, exceeding several earlier small-vessel approaches. The causal reason: combining Neo-M8N accuracy and two-hop LoRa preserved position fidelity and timeliness, whereas prior methods usually compromised one of those elements. Below we compare with selected prior systems and show why the improvements occur.

Table IV shows direct comparisons. Compared to Apriani et al. [5], who reported 89.2% at 1 km using single-hop LoRa, our two-hop chain improves packet delivery and thus classification because the repeater reduces instances where a single obstructed path would drop a packet. Compared to Chen et al. [7] whose u-blox M8 tests produced high GNSS fidelity but lacked fielded radio forwarding, our work matches GNSS accuracy while adding end-to-end reporting. Hadi and Arsana's [4] older Neo-6M Arduino alarm had long cold-start times (several minutes) and no remote logging; that explains their 3,000 ms effective latency in practical use. Our latency is higher than smartphone-only systems in ideal local networks (Sen et al. [8]) because LoRa airtime dominates; still, our architecture is more suitable where cellular networks are unavailable.

content.text: Headline: The transmitter ran 6.3 hours under continuous 5 s reporting on 2x18650 2,400 mAh cells; the repeater and receiver ran approximately 17 h and 16 h respectively. We ran stress tests including simulated communication dropouts, temperature swings, and overloads to evaluate recovery behavior and drift. The goal was to see how the prototype behaves during extended unattended operation and under incident scenarios (simulated interference or reconnect events).

As shown in Table V, the most challenging condition was simulated network dropout under high wave interference where packet loss peaked; the gateway and Python subscriber were designed to accept re-ordered packets and re-apply sequence checks, which allowed auto-recovery within 200 ms on average. The thermal cycling test revealed minor GNSS drift (0.25 m) after prolonged heating, which is acceptable for our 20 m violation threshold but worth monitoring in tropical deployments.

content.Title: Time-Series System Response
content.Prompt: A multi-line time-series chart of RSSI (dBm), SNR (dB), and zone status over a 600-second trial. Horizontal axis labeled "Time (s)" from 0 to 600. Primary vertical axis on left for RSSI (range -110 to -30 dBm) with a blue line plotted (sampled every 5 s). Secondary vertical axis on right for SNR (range -20 to 15 dB) with an orange line. Overlay a stepped red/green band at top showing zone status (green=Safe, yellow=Alert, red=Violation) with transition markers. Annotate key events: "packet loss spike at 420 s", "buzzer on at 312 s" and mark them with vertical dashed lines and text. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: We built and field-tested a LoRa-MQTT geofencing notification system for Indonesian fishing vessels using ESP32 controllers, u-blox Neo-M8N GNSS, and SX1278 Ra-02 radios. The prototype met the main operational metrics: Neo-M8N mean positional error 1.62 m (cold start 5–7 s), Neo-6M mean error 3.04 m (cold start up to 525 s) which guided the Neo-M8N selection; LoRa two-hop chains maintained 0% packet loss and mean end-to-end latency 1.55 s up to 2 km on the north coast; at 3 km packet delivery fell (north coast success ~79.4%) and south-coast noisy conditions produced packet loss up to 13.2% at 2 km. The geofence classifier achieved 95.4% accuracy and F1 = 0.947, which exceeds the 90% deployment target and shows the determinant-plus-distance approach with hysteresis is effective for real boats and coastal geometries.

Limitations are honest and operationally important. First, high sea states and spray on the south coast reduced SNR and increased packet loss; in such scenarios the prototype must be augmented with higher-gain mast antennas or alternative radio bands (70 cm vs 433 MHz) and perhaps a second redundant gateway. Second, the planar line-crossing approximation can misclassify when geofence segments exceed several kilometers or when vessels operate very far offshore; a geodesic/haversine-based computation would be required for wide-area boundaries. Third, battery endurance (transmitter 6.3 h) limits continuous multi-day deployment without supplemental charging or larger capacity cells; solar trickle charging or removable battery packs are practical mitigations.

Specific future work directions: (1) implement geodesic-aware geofencing using great-circle computations and integrate DGPS/RTK corrections when available to push classification error below 1 m; (2) evaluate alternative radio topologies and antenna arrays (directional mast, 6 dBi to 9 dBi) to improve 3+ km coverage in south-coast conditions and test 868/915 MHz variants; (3) integrate lightweight cryptographic signing of JSON payloads (ECC) and broker authentication to prevent spoofing in contested waters; (4) extend the dashboard to include automated alert escalation (SMS/Voice to authorities) and store-and-forward buffering in gateway for intermittent backhaul; (5) run a multi-week pilot fleet deployment across multiple districts (North Natuna, Semarang) to measure operational false-alarm rates under routine fishing patterns. These steps are actionable and would bring the prototype closer to operational adoption by KKP and local authority partners.
